title: Spatial Saturation and Tree Senescence in the Carlos Spegazzini Botanical Garden: An 87-Year Aerial and GIS Analysis (1939–2026)
content: Botanical gardens are repositories of biodiversity and heritage, yet their sustainability is threatened by canopy closure and spatial saturation. This study analyzes 87 years (1939–2026) of structural dynamics in the Carlos Spegazzini Botanical Garden (La Plata, Argentina). We combined historical aerial photo interpretation, field censuses (535 trees), allometric modeling, and spatial competition analyses (Voronoi polygons, nearest-neighbor distances, Clark-Evans index). Tree density decreased from 185.0 to 119.5 ind/ha, while canopy cover increased from 44.6% to 102.4%, with estimated crown cover peaking at 202.2%, well above the 70% saturation threshold. Crown radii increased significantly (Kruskal-Wallis χ² = 492.95, p < 0.001), and the Clark-Evans index confirmed a clustered distribution (R = 0.620, p < 0.001). Of the 535 individuals, 218 (40.7%) were heritage trees, with 78.9% in good sanitary condition and 46 requiring urgent care. Despite intense crown overlap, the 5.6% mortality (2022–2026) was not explained by spatial variables (pseudo-R² = 0.0038; AUC = 0.481). Pathogens, mechanical damage, or senescence would be the primary drivers. We recommend selective thinning, priority phytosanitary care, a necropsy protocol, gradual renewal, and density targets of 120–150 ind/ha to balance ecological functioning with heritage preservation.
